title: American Airlines 383

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Uncontained Engine Failure and Subsequent Fire

summary: American Airlines Flight 383 suffered an uncontained right engine failure during takeoff roll at O'Hare on October 28, 2016. The HPT stage 2 disk ruptured, penetrating the wing fuel tank and causing a severe fire. Captain rejected takeoff and crew evacuated all 170 occupants; 21 sustained injuries.
probable_cause: The probable cause was the failure of the high-pressure turbine stage 2 disk, which severed the main engine fuel feed line and breached the right main wing fuel tank, releasing fuel that resulted in a fire during the takeoff roll. The HPT stage 2 disk failed because of low-cycle fatigue cracks that initiated from an internal subsurface manufacturing anomaly that was most likely not detectable during production and in-service inspections. Contributing factors included lack of a separate engine fire checklist for ground operations and lack of communication between flight and cabin crews.

factors.evidence: HPT stage 2 disk rupture during takeoff power at 1431:43.4 when airspeed was 128 knots; sudden engine imbalance detected (p. 2, 16).
Right engine suffered uncontained failure with disk fragment penetrating inboard section of right wing, severing fuel feed line and breaching fuel tank (p. 1, 2).
HPT stage 2 disk had discrete dirty white spot manufacturing anomaly undetectable by production inspection methods; fatigue cracks not detectable at last in-service inspection (p. 75).
Severe fire on right side of airplane following engine failure and fuel tank breach (p. 1, 2).

events.text: Tower controller cleared airplane for takeoff; first officer acknowledged (p. 1).
At 14:31:19, CVR recorded sound of increasing engine RPM; at 14:31:24 engines achieved takeoff power (p. 1-2).
At 14:31:32, first officer made routine callout of 80 knots airspeed; crew described spool-up as normal (p. 2).
At 14:31:43.4, with 128 knots indicated, longitudinal acceleration decreased suddenly from 0.23 to 0.13 G; CVR recorded 'bang' sound (p. 2).
Captain initiated rejected takeoff maneuver; throttles moved to idle at 14:31:45.6 (p. 2).
Autobrakes activated at rejected takeoff airspeed of 134 knots (V1); speedbrakes activated about 2 seconds later (p. 2).
At 14:31:50, first officer contacted ATC stating airplane stopping on runway; controller responded with fire warning (p. 2).
At 14:32:00, CVR recorded engine fire warning; FDR showed 'ENG FIRE R' annunciated; airplane decelerated to 35 knots (p. 2-3).
At 14:32:04.1, captain called for engine fire checklist (20.6 seconds after engine failure); fuel switch shut off (p. 3).
FDR showed airplane came to stop at 14:32:09.8, 26.4 seconds after engine failure; captain could smell smoke (p. 3).

recommendations.text: Establish and lead an industry group to evaluate current and enhanced inspection technologies for nickel alloys and issue guidance for nickel alloy rotating engine components.
Require subsurface in-service inspection techniques such as ultrasonic inspections for critical high-energy, life-limited rotating parts for all engines.
Revise Advisory Circular 20-128A to minimize hazards from uncontained engine failures based on analysis of recent uncontained engine failure data.
Require operators to develop emergency checklist procedures for engine fire on the ground to expeditiously address fire hazard.
Develop guidance for flight attendant training regarding assessing exits during emergencies and identifying conditions that preclude opening exits.
Review training programs to ensure flight attendants and crews receive training on different interphone systems.
Conduct research on effects of carry-on baggage on evacuation times and identify countermeasures.
Work with operators to develop engine fire checklist procedures for ground operations.
Review engine fire checklists and ensure procedures expeditiously address ground engine fires without delaying evacuation.
